subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Commodity Speculation
description: A micro-lesson that makes Commodity Speculation usable.

hook.text: Hedge funds and investment banks trade billions in coffee futures without ever touching a single bean.

buildup.text: Speculators buy and sell contracts to profit from price movements. Their volume dwarfs actual coffee trade.

discovery.text: This liquidity helps large buyers hedge risk—but it also amplifies price swings that hurt small farmers.

twist.text: In 2010, speculation drove coffee futures up 77% in one year. Supply and demand alone didn't justify the spike.

climax.text: The debate continues: do financial markets help or hurt the real coffee economy? There's no simple answer.

punchline.text: Wall Street trades coffee faster than farmers can grow it.

quiz.question: How did commodity speculation affect coffee prices in 2010?
options: Prices rose 77%, partly driven by speculative trading

details.summary: Financial speculators trade coffee futures without intending to buy actual beans. Their activity can amplify price swings far beyond what supply and demand would cause. Some analysts estimate that speculative trades outnumber physical coffee transactions by a factor of ten or more.
details.whyItMatters: Speculation adds volatility that hurts farmers while providing no benefit to the physical coffee supply chain. It is a structural flaw in how coffee is priced.
takeaways: Speculators trade coffee futures without buying physical beans
Speculative volume can far exceed actual coffee transactions
This amplifies price volatility beyond supply-demand fundamentals

faq.question: How do coffee futures work in practice?
faq.answer: Futures are contracts to buy or sell coffee at a set price on a future date. Producers use them to lock in prices and manage risk. Speculators buy and sell contracts for profit without ever handling coffee, adding liquidity but also volatility to the market.

faq.question: Does speculation make coffee more expensive?
faq.answer: It can push prices in either direction. During bullish speculation, prices rise above fair value. During bearish sentiment, prices drop below production costs. Consumers are somewhat insulated because retail prices adjust slowly, but farmers feel the impact immediately.
